title: Unravelling the Microplastic Footprint of Fertilizers in Agroecosystems: Sources, Transformation, Environmental Fate and Management
content: Fertilizers are increasingly recognised as a pathway for microplastic (MP) entry into agricultural systems. This review critically evaluates the sources, formation mechanisms, characteristics, fate, environmental implications, analytical challenges, and mitigation options associated with fertilizer-derived MPs. Polymer-coated controlled-release fertilizers generate MPs through coating deterioration, including cracking, abrasion, wetting and drying, photooxidation under sunlight exposure, and polymer-specific biological transformation. Organic fertilizers, composts, digestates, biosolids, and manure-based amendments may also introduce pre-existing MPs originating from contaminated waste streams. Evidence from China, Bangladesh, Europe, the United Kingdom, and Japan confirms fertilizer-associated MP occurrence. However, source attribution is often complicated by mulch films, irrigation infrastructure, packaging, atmospheric deposition, and historical soil contamination. Japanese paddy systems provide the strongest field evidence for direct release, retention, and hydrological export of coated-fertilizer microcapsules. Fertilizer-derived MPs may persist in soil, fragment into smaller particles, redistribute vertically, and move through runoff and drainage. Experimental studies indicate possible effects on soil chemistry, microbial communities, enzyme activities, cadmium availability, and early crop establishment; however, many studies use concentrations exceeding field-relevant exposure levels. Evidence directly linking fertilizer-derived MPs to uptake by edible crops or human exposure remains insufficient. Analytical inconsistencies, especially in recovery efficiency, particle-size limits, polymer identification, and source attribution, further constrain comparison across studies. Bio-based and biodegradable coatings are promising alternatives but require verification of soil mineralization, residual-particle formation, additive safety, and field performance. Future research should prioritise source-resolved field mass balances, standardised analytical workflows, realistic exposure experiments, and life-cycle evaluation of alternative fertilizer technologies.
